newsitem.title: UK: Adams seeks UK N.Irish talks pledge.
newsitem.headline: Adams seeks UK N.Irish talks pledge.

text.p: Gerry Adams, leader of the IRA's political wing, challenged Britain on Tuesday to give a cast-iron guarantee of direct entry to talks for his Sinn Fein party if the Irish guerrilla force abandons violence.
Adams told the nationalist Irish News daily that if Britain gave clear assurances about viable all-party negotiations, Northern Ireland's floundering peace process could be restored.

In a direct response to a speech by new Prime Minister Tony Blair last Friday, Adams said Britain "should state clearly that Sinn Fein will join the negotiations immediately following an unequivocal restoration of the IRA (Irish Republican Army) cessation of August 1994".
Blair gave the go-ahead for fresh talks between Sinn Fein and government officials but said the IRA must fully forsake violence for Sinn Fein to get into full negotiations.
His initiative was aimed at breaking a deadlock that blighted Sinn Fein's relations with the previous British prime minister, John Major, for 18 months.

Sinn Fein has consistently demanded immediate entry and warned against a "decontamination period" that would delay access to talks in the event of its IRA ally declaring a fresh ceasefire for one that collapsed in February last year.
Blair gave a stern last-chance warning to Sinn Fein and the IRA to demonstrate a "words and deeds" commitment to peaceful methods to gain a voice in peace talks.
Adams rounded on Blair for strongly defending Northern Ireland's union with Britain but also signalled his belief that any fresh IRA ceasefire would be unequivocal.

Political correspondent William Graham, quoting from an article by Adams for The Irish News, wrote :"Significantly, Mr Adams went further and said: 'Sinn Fein believes that an unequivocal restoration of the IRA cessation would represent the most important confidence building initiative on the IRA's part.'"
The 60 per cent Protestant majority want to stay British but the 40 per cent Roman Catholics, some of whom support the IRA, want an United Ireland freed of London's influence.
Adams said Blair's speech was "barren of new thinking" and that "nationalists felt disturbed to hear Mr Blair declare himself a unionist with such gusto."
In his Belfast address Blair, whose Labour Party succeeded Major's Conservatives on May 1 pledged that the province would remain under London while a majority supported it.
